note: Curated subset covering the techniques present in the TriageMate dataset.

techniques.name: OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
techniques.description: Adversaries read the memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) to extract credentials such as password hashes and Kerberos tickets. Tools include Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, and procdump.
techniques.detection: Watch for non-system processes opening a handle to lsass.exe with high access rights, and for rundll32 calling comsvcs.dll MiniDump.
techniques.investigation: Confirm which process accessed LSASS, whether it is signed and expected, and whether credentials may now be compromised.

techniques.name: OS Credential Dumping: SAM
techniques.description: Adversaries copy the Security Account Manager (SAM) registry hive to extract local account password hashes, using tools like reg save, esentutl, or Mimikatz.
techniques.detection: Watch for reg.exe or esentutl.exe accessing the SAM hive, or registry hive copies.
techniques.investigation: Check which account ran the copy, whether it was an administrator, and whether local hashes should be considered exposed.

techniques.name: OS Credential Dumping: NTDS
techniques.description: Adversaries extract the Active Directory database (NTDS.dit) from a domain controller to obtain every domain account hash, using ntdsutil, NinjaCopy, or volume shadow copies.
techniques.detection: Watch for ntdsutil, use of volume shadow copies to access NTDS.dit, and large file reads on domain controllers.
techniques.investigation: On a DC this is critical. Confirm the operator, and treat the whole domain as potentially compromised if confirmed.

techniques.name: OS Credential Dumping: LSA Secrets
techniques.description: Adversaries read LSA secrets from the registry to obtain service account passwords and cached credentials.
techniques.detection: Watch for access to the SECURITY registry hive and secretsdump-style tooling.
techniques.investigation: Identify exposed service accounts and rotate their credentials.

techniques.name: OS Credential Dumping: DCSync
techniques.description: Adversaries abuse the directory replication (DRSUAPI) protocol to request password data from a domain controller as if they were another DC, using Mimikatz or Covenant.
techniques.detection: Watch for DRSUAPI DsGetNCChanges replication requests from hosts that are not domain controllers.
techniques.investigation: Confirm the requesting host is not a legitimate DC. If not, treat as a domain compromise.

techniques.name: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
techniques.description: Adversaries use SMB and admin shares (ADMIN$, C$) to move laterally, often with PsExec or SMBExec, installing a temporary service to run commands remotely.
techniques.detection: Watch for service creation events (EventID 7045) with random or temporary service names, and remote execution over SMB.
techniques.investigation: Identify the source host, confirm whether the admin action was authorized, and check what ran on the destination.

techniques.name: Remote Services: Distributed Component Object Model
techniques.description: Adversaries use DCOM to execute code on remote hosts, for example through Excel macros or ShellWindows objects.
techniques.detection: Watch for mmc.exe, excel.exe, or iexplore.exe spawning script interpreters on a remote host.
techniques.investigation: Confirm whether the Office or COM activity was user-initiated and expected.

techniques.name: Remote Services: Windows Remote Management
techniques.description: Adversaries use WinRM and PowerShell Remoting to run commands on remote hosts.
techniques.detection: Watch for wsmprovhost.exe spawning processes, and PowerShell remoting sessions from unexpected hosts.
techniques.investigation: Confirm the remoting session was from an authorized admin host.

techniques.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
techniques.description: Adversaries use WMI to execute commands locally or on remote hosts, often spawning processes from WmiPrvSE.exe.
techniques.detection: Watch for WmiPrvSE.exe spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe, especially from a remote trigger.
techniques.investigation: Determine the source of the WMI call and whether it was legitimate management traffic.

techniques.name: Scheduled Task
techniques.description: Adversaries create or modify scheduled tasks to execute code, for persistence or to run on a remote host.
techniques.detection: Watch for schtasks.exe /create, and new tasks pointing at scripts or unusual binaries.
techniques.investigation: Confirm whether the task was created by an administrator for a legitimate purpose.

techniques.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
techniques.description: Adversaries request Kerberos service tickets to crack service account passwords offline, using tools like Rubeus.
techniques.detection: Watch for Rubeus execution and large numbers of Kerberos TGS requests.
techniques.investigation: Identify targeted service accounts and consider rotating their passwords.

techniques.name: Input Capture: GUI Input Capture
techniques.description: Adversaries present a fake credential prompt to trick a user into entering their password.
techniques.detection: Watch for scripts calling Get-Credential or creating credential dialog prompts.
techniques.investigation: Confirm whether the prompt was legitimate and whether the user entered credentials.

techniques.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager
techniques.description: Adversaries read stored credentials from the Windows Vault / Credential Manager.
techniques.detection: Watch for access to Vault files and vaultcmd.exe usage.
techniques.investigation: Identify which stored credentials may have been read.

techniques.name: Exploitation of Remote Services
techniques.description: Adversaries exploit vulnerabilities in remote services to move laterally, for example the Zerologon vulnerability (CVE-2020-1472) against domain controllers.
techniques.detection: Watch for anomalous NetrServerAuthenticate2 traffic and known exploit signatures.
techniques.investigation: Confirm whether the target service is patched and whether exploitation succeeded.

techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
techniques.description: Adversaries use PowerShell to execute commands and scripts, often obfuscated or encoded to evade detection.
techniques.detection: Watch for powershell.exe with -enc, -exec bypass, obfuscation, or launched by unusual parents like rundll32.
techniques.investigation: Decode the script if possible, and determine what it did. Confirm whether the activity was authorized.

techniques.name: Inhibit System Recovery
techniques.description: Adversaries delete backups and volume shadow copies so victims cannot recover, a hallmark of ransomware. Tools include vssadmin, wmic shadowcopy delete, wbadmin, and bcdedit.
techniques.detection: Watch for vssadmin delete shadows, wmic shadowcopy delete, wbadmin delete catalog, and bcdedit recovery changes.
techniques.investigation: Treat as a likely ransomware precursor. Isolate the host and check for encryption activity and the initial access vector.

techniques.name: Data Encrypted for Impact
techniques.description: Adversaries encrypt files to extort the victim (ransomware), often after deleting backups.
techniques.detection: Watch for mass file renames or extension changes, ransom notes, and high-volume file writes.
techniques.investigation: Isolate the host immediately, identify the ransomware family, and check backup integrity.
